title: TrueNorth
intro: TrueNorth is IBM's neuromorphic chip, developed under the DARPA SyNAPSE program and published by Merolla et al. in Science in 2014. It packs a million spiking neurons and 256 million synapses onto one chip that draws about 70 milliwatts while running in real time. Its design is a clean example of the tiled neurosynaptic core, and of the trade-off between efficiency and flexibility: its synapses are fixed, so all learning happens offline.

items: Scale: 5.4 billion transistors in a 28 nm process, organized as a 64 × 64 array of 4096 neurosynaptic cores.

The core: each core is a crossbar of 256 input axons and 256 output neurons. At each of the 65,536 crossings, a binary synapse is either connected or not. Each axon has one of four types, and each neuron has its own signed weight for each axon type, so the effective weight of a synapse is the neuron's weight for that axon's type. Crossbar memory, neuron parameters and routing tables all sit in the core: colocated memory and compute.

Neurons: a configurable digital integrate-and-fire model with leak, thresholds (optionally stochastic), and several reset modes. It can reproduce many of the Izhikevich firing patterns through combinations of neurons.

Communication: when a neuron fires, its spike becomes an address event routed across a 2-D mesh to one axon of one target core. Each neuron has exactly one target axon, so fan-out is achieved by duplicating neurons, a real constraint when mapping networks.
Timing: spikes are processed asynchronously and event-driven within cores, but the chip advances in a global 1 kHz tick, giving deterministic, one-to-one equivalence with a software simulator.
Power: about 65-70 mW for typical real-time networks, roughly 26 picojoules per synaptic event. That is orders of magnitude below a CPU running the same network.

Scaling: chips tile seamlessly. The NS16e board put 16 chips in a 4 × 4 array (16 million neurons, 4 billion synapses, about 2.5 W for the chips), and one went to Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in 2016. The NS16e-4, ordered by the US Air Force Research Laboratory in 2017, ran four such boards in one enclosure: 64 chips, 64 million neurons and 16 billion synapses. These are the largest TrueNorth systems on record; the rack-scale machines sometimes mentioned were plans, not documented deployments.

blocks.text: Networks are composed from "corelets", reusable blocks of configured cores, in IBM's programming environment. To run deep networks, Esser et al. (2016) introduced Eedn (energy-efficient deep neuromorphic networks), which trains convolutional networks with constraints matching TrueNorth (trinary weights, binary spikes, limited fan-in) and then maps them to the chip. They reported near state-of-the-art accuracy on several image and audio datasets at about 1200-2600 frames per second while drawing 25-275 mW (more than 6000 frames per second per watt). Demonstrations included real-time object detection in video and gesture recognition from an event camera (Amir et al. 2017).

items: Very low power and deterministic behavior make it attractive for embedded inference.
No on-chip learning: synapses are fixed once programmed. Online adaptation, STDP and three-factor rules are not possible on the chip itself.
Binary crossbar synapses with shared weights per axon type, and one target per neuron, mean networks need careful restructuring to fit.
IBM's later NorthPole chip (2023) moved away from spiking, keeping the colocated memory-compute idea for conventional neural network inference.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: TrueNorth's lesson is architectural. A neurosynaptic core with 256 inputs and 256 neurons is close to the size of a cortical minicolumn group, and its event-driven, local-memory design is the right template. But a Thousand Brains column learns continually from movement and sensation, which needs on-chip plasticity. For a learning column, look at Loihi, SpiNNaker or an FPGA. Use TrueNorth-style constraints (low-precision weights, limited fan-in) as design discipline.
